title: "Practical tips"
---

## General practical tips

As we come to the end of this tutorial, you should feel more
knowledgeable and confident about preregistration and how to carry out
one in your own research. Even if you are not quite ready to implement a
study preregistration just yet, you should have the tools to critically
evaluate your own research planning approaches and existing
preregistered studies. Below are four practical tips and additional
resources to help you on your next steps on your preregistration
journey!

### Tip 1: Find an appropriate template

A good way to get started with a preregistration is to find a template
that aligns well with your research area and standards in your
discipline. You can refer back to section X where examples of
preregistration templates are listed.

### Tip 2: Evaluate existing preregistrations

Spending time reading and evaluating existing preregistrations can get
you thinking critically about what is included in one, level of detail,
etc. Reviewing other researcher's preregistered studies can act as a
blueprint for when you come to write yours.

You can find an example of a preregistered study in your own research
area on the Open Science Framework’s Zotero library. You can filter for
subject matter and study type.
<https://www.zotero.org/groups/479248/osf/collections/VKXUAZM7> 

### Tip 3: Embrace change and mistakes

As researchers we are not perfect and our studies can change when we are
presented with new information [@bishop2018]. Your first preregistration
is likely to have mistakes or information left out. That is ok! Think
about how you can take the process of writing a preregistration as a
learning opportunity and build your knowledge and make improvements for
the next one.

### Tip 4: Add more Open Science practices to your research workflows

Preregistration is one of many Open Science practices! In addition to
preregistrering your study, you can make your research even more
transparent and reproducible with open data (anonymized as appropriate),
open code. You can read more about how to integrate Open Science
practices in your workflows in the OSC's [Research Cycle
Handbook](https://www.osc.lmu.de/training/research-cycle-handbook.html).
